newsitem.title: UK: Markets right to fear central bank gold sales - UBS.
newsitem.headline: Markets right to fear central bank gold sales - UBS.

text.p: Bullion markets were probably right to expect European central banks to sell gold reserves to qualify for a single currency, according to analyst Andy Smith of Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS).

But these sales might not be imminent, and might constitute only a small fraction of central bank holdings, Smith said in a study on Wednesday entitled "Central Bank gold: the Picture of Less Reserve".
There were other ways of raising money than selling gold, he said.
"Where gold is undervalued on the books at well below market prices, the prize of reducing net debt by realising a capital gain on gold might be more tempting still," Smith said.

Gold sales were easier to arrange than public asset privatisations, and, amid the highest post-war levels of European unemployment, "they are likely to raise less public ire than tax increases or spending cuts".

The market has been on tenterhooks since Belgian and Dutch central banks sold gold from their reserves in 1996 and at the beginning of 1997 respectively. Since 1989, the two sold a total of 1,107 tonnes of gold.
Gold analysts say prices are unlikely to show any significant rises from the current $350 an ounce level while the prospect of central bank sales continues to haunt the market.

To qualify for a single currency, European countries must reduce the share of their public deficit in the total gross domestic product (GDP) to three percent, and the ratio of total debt to GDP to 60 percent.
Smith said the impact for gold could be less severe than initially apparent since the entry criteria were likely to be "made of rubber and set in elastic clauses".

But fear of pre-entry gold sales would remain. If a slowdown in European economic activity this year was was not enough to allow EMU entry through "exceptional clauses" and if entry depended on simply being able to trim debt/GDP ratios, central banks could be tempted to part with their gold.

"Would-be members might have to run to stand still, selling assets quickly to chase a moving, lower GDP denominator," Smith said, adding that pre-EMU pressure might intensify in the last quarter of 1997.
But the pressure for gold sales would be delayed or eased by a postponement of the whole process or the exclusion of some important gold holders from the first round membership list.

Seven countries currently earmarked for the first round of EMU, including France, Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium, hold a total 8,955 tonnes of gold in their central bank coffers. UBS estimated that to offset a shortfall of one percent in the debt/GDP ratio, these would have to sell 3,900 tonnes of gold.
Given that such large amounts of gold could not be dumped without wrecking the price, there would be an incentive to sell first, Smith said.

But after May 1998, when the qualification should be completed "rather, a hangover of reserves (dollars and gold) will remain after monetary union, to be sweated out, probably over a number of years."
